function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files and shell commands that will get the **nodejs‑welcome** repository up‑and‑running in Docker/Kubernetes and automatically build on every push to `main`.  
Feel free to copy‑paste the snippets into your local clone of the repo.

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH access, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣  Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1  Dockerfile

The repo is a simple Express app (`app.js` + `package.json`).  
A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# 1️⃣  Use a lightweight Node.js base image
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# 2️⃣  Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# 3️⃣  Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 4️⃣  Copy source code
COPY . .

# 5️⃣  Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 6️⃣  Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` guarantees a clean, reproducible install.  
> * The container listens on port **3000** – the default for the sample app.

> **Save** this file as `Dockerfile` in the repo root.

---

### 2.2  Kubernetes YAML

Below is a single `deployment.yaml` that contains both the Deployment and Service definitions.  
It uses the image that will be built by the GitHub Actions workflow (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Where to put it?**  
> Create a folder called `k8s` (or `deployments`) at the repo root and place the file there.

---

### 2.3  GitHub Actions workflow

Create a workflow that:

1. Builds the Docker image.  
2. Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).  
3. (Optional) Deploys to a cluster – you can add a `kubectl apply` step if you have a cluster configured.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GHCR
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest .
          docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # (Optional) Deploy to a cluster
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      #   with:
      #     manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
      #     images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important** – The workflow uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> No extra secrets are required unless you want to push to a different registry.

> **Save** this file as `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`.

---

## 3️⃣  Add, commit, and push the changes

```bash
# Stage all new/modified files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

> After the push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to GHCR.

---

## 4️⃣  Verify

1. **Check the Actions tab** – you should see a successful run.  
2. **Pull the image** (optional):

   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
   ```

3. **Deploy locally** (optional):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

   Then expose the service (e.g., via `kubectl port-forward svc/nodejs-welcome 8080:80`) and visit `http://localhost:8080`.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A production‑ready Dockerfile for the Node.js app.  
- Kubernetes Deployment & Service YAMLs.  
- A GitHub Actions workflow that builds and pushes the image on every push to `main`.  
- All changes committed and pushed to the repo.

Happy coding!
